TADĀŃJA VAJRAṆE SARVA VIKARAṆA VINAYAKAṆA VARAYA MAHĀGHAṆE PARDHE VIDANTA KARAYA HŪṂ PHAṬ KURU DHĀRAṆAYE SVĀHĀ.
Recite "Hā" three times; this is the mantra for bathing. As for the empowerment mantra, one should perform self-empowerment using this mantra and the mudrā.

The mantra is: “Oṃ hāḥ khari ri hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this consecration mantra three times. As for the mudrā: interlace the two little fingers and insert them into the palms; press the two ring fingers together upon the crossed little fingers so they enter the palms; stand the tips of the two middle fingers upright and touching each other; press the two index fingers onto the upper joints of the two middle fingers, causing the middle joints of the index fingers to bend; and place the two thumbs alongside the sides of the two index fingers.
Taking water with the mudrā, recite the mantra three times and perform self-consecration; this is the consecration mudrā.
Next, bind your hair yourself using the mantra and hand-mudrā.

The mantra is: "Oṃ susiddhi-kari svāhā. Recite this three times; it is the mantra for binding the hair, applicable to all three families (*trikula*). As for the mudrā: form a fist with the right hand and extend the thumb straight. Bend the index finger and press its tip against the top of the thumb, causing the index finger to curve into a circle.
Form this mudrā, recite the mantra three times, and place it upon the crown of the head; this constitutes the binding of the hair. This is the Hair-Binding Mudrā.
Furthermore, the Hair-Binding Mantra of the Buddha Family is:
"Oṃ śikhi śikhe svāhā. Recite this three times. Furthermore, the Hair-Binding Mantra of the Lotus Family is:
Recite "Oṃ śikhe svāhā" three times. The mantra for binding the hair of the Vajra family is: "Oṃ śikhāya svāhā. Recite this three times.

Whenever bathing, one should not bathe in muddy water, nor in water containing thorns, nor in suspended or swift-flowing water, nor in narrow channels or shallow water, nor in whirlpools or rapids, nor in turbid water teeming with insects, nor in irrigation water, nor in water from pits. One must not bathe in such waters as these.

Furthermore, one should not defecate or urinate in the water or on its banks; nor should one leap, run, swim, or float about playfully in the water. One should remain still within the water and not gaze at private parts, nor should one mentally dwell upon the private parts, waist, breasts, or any other limbs of women.
One should bathe in silence and stillness, merely to remove impurities and without the thought of adorning the body.

Regarding the offering of three handfuls of water: once the bath is completed, face the direction where the deity resides, visualize the deity, recite the mantra, and perform the mudrā; then, using the mudrā, take up the water in your cupped hands and offer it.

One should visualize bathing the Honzon and offering *argha* water; within the water, there may be three kinds of signs: if the water reaches the knees, it is called the lower sign; if it reaches the navel, it is the middle sign; and if it reaches the neck, it is the superior sign. Reciting the mantra according to one's intention amidst these three waters, one should then proceed to the *dōjō*.

The mantra for offering water to the Buddha Family is: “Oṃ tretaye buddha svāhā. Recite this three times; this is the mantra for offering three handfuls of water to the Buddha Family. Furthermore, the mantra for offering water to the Lotus Family is:
“Oṃ bari bari hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this three times; this is the mantra for offering three handfuls of water to the Lotus Family. Furthermore, the mantra for offering water to the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ viśvavajri svāhā. Recite this three times; this is the mantra for offering three handfuls of water to the Vajra Family. The mudrā common to the three families is as follows: place both hands flat and palms upward, with the sides touching; join the tips of the two index fingers with the tips of the two thumbs, while the remaining six fingers are slightly bent.

Taking water in the hollow of the hands with the mudrā, recite the mantra three times and offer it as a bath to the Honzon; this is the general hand-mudrā for offering three handfuls of water common to the three families (*tri-kula*).
Regarding "proceeding to the divine chamber": when entering toward the ritual hall (*dōjō*), do not give rise to anger or greed, but proceed while focusing one-pointedly on the Honzon.

Within this [mandala], one must not step over weapons or various medicinal herbs—namely, diverse vessels, mounts, bells, seals, withered flowers, medicinal essences, and all grasses and trees; nor should one step over the shadows of caityas, honored images, or bhikṣus. Furthermore, one must not ride upon elephants, horses, camels, oxen, sheep, donkeys, or any other vehicles, nor should one tread upon painted images, seals, and the like, or allow the hands and body to touch them. If one violates these [precepts], one falls from the samaya.
One should also not give rise to greed, hatred, delusion, pride, restlessness, or arrogance.

When entering a shrine room while wearing wooden sandals, upon encountering a caitya, a venerable teacher, or a temple, one should remove the sandals and pay due respect before proceeding to the place of practice.

Next, regarding changing clothes and sprinkling the body: this refers to washing the hands and feet six times outside the entrance of the *maṇḍala*, using the previously explained *dhāraṇī* and mudrā for purifying protection, drinking water, and wiping the lips as before.
Having once again drunk water and performed the ritual sprinkling for purification (*śodhana*), one should then proceed according to the practice; this applies to all three families (*kula*).
Furthermore, the mantra for drinking water and sprinkling for purification in the Buddha Family (*buddhakula*) is:

"Oṃ mahāvajra hūṃ. This is the mantra for the water for purification in the Buddha Family. Furthermore, the mantra for drinking water and sprinkling for purification in the Lotus Family (*padmakula*) is:

"Oṃ dhuṭa dhuṭa ra kuru kuru svāhā. This is the mantra for sprinkling purification (*prokṣaṇa*) belonging to the Lotus Family (*padmakula*). Furthermore, the mantra for drinking water and sprinkling purification belonging to the Vajra Family (*vajrakula*) is:

"Oṃ jvalitavajri hūṃ. This is the mantra for sprinkling purification belonging to the Vajra Family. Furthermore, the hand gesture (*mudrā*) for drinking water and sprinkling purification belonging to the Buddha Family (*buddhakula*) is explained as follows: extend the right hand upward, bend the ring finger inward, and do not let it touch the palm; this is the water-gesture for sprinkling purification belonging to the Buddha Family.

Furthermore, regarding the mudrā for sprinkling water for purification in the Lotus Family: extend the right hand upward with the ring finger pointing inward and the palm not touching anything; spread the index and little fingers apart—this is the water-sprinkling purification mudrā of the Vajra Family.
Next, purify the garment bestowed outside the gate by means of mantra and mudrā.
The mantra is: "Oṃ vimara svāhā.

This is the mantra for purifying and changing garments. As for the form of the mudrā: clench the right hand into a fist, take water while reciting the mantra, and sprinkle it upon the garment. This is the mudrā for purifying and changing garments.
Next, one should don the robe after consecrating it with the mantra.

The mantra is: "Oṃ parivāra-pavitrīṇi hūṃ. This is the mantra for donning the robe; there is no mudrā. Regarding "entering the room and performing prostrations," as explained in the instructions, the practitioner should enter the divine chamber with a single-minded focus.

Having entered the room, one should face the Honored One, join the palms, and bow the body, though the head need not touch the ground. First, within the room, one should place an image of the Honored One, or a *caitya*, or simply a seat; having entered and performed prostration, one should then make offerings to it.

Regarding the preparation of the ritual implements: these refer to the five types beginning with fragrant ointments (*vilepana*), the *gorocana* (cow-gallstone), the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), the grass ring (*dūrvāvalaya*), one’s own seat, the *argha* vessel, white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*), the waist-thread (*mekhalā*), and so forth. These are called the ritual implements and should be prepared beforehand.
When entering the chamber, one should enter while reciting the mantra aloud. The mantra is:
"Oṃ jvalita rocani hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for entering the chamber, common to all three families (*trikula*). Next, one should perform the *samaya* mantra and mudrā.
The mantra of the first, the Buddha Family, is:

"Oṃ tathāgatodbhava svāhā. Recite this five times; this is the *samaya* mantra of the Buddha Family. As for the mudrā: turn both hands upward, extend all ten fingers straight forward with the sides touching each other, and slightly bend the upper joints of the two index fingers. This is the *samaya* mudrā of the Buddha Family.
Next, the *samaya* mantra and mudrā of the Padma-kula are explained. The mantra is: "Oṃ pañca-namo-bhagavate svāhā. Recite this five times;

this is the *samaya* mantra of the Padma-kula. As for the mudrā: first, join the palms together. Then, extend the six fingers of both hands outward so that they do not touch one another, while the thumbs and little fingers of both hands remain joined as before. Make the palms hollow like an opening lotus flower and slightly bend the six middle fingers. This is the *samaya* mudrā of the Padma-kula.
Next, the *samaya* mantra and hand-seal (*mudrā*) of the Vajra Family are explained.

The mantra is: "Oṃ vajranābāya svāhā. Recite this five times; this is the *samaya* mantra of the Vajra Family. As for the form of the hand-seal: place the right hand over the left, with the backs of both hands joined together. Interlace the thumb of the right hand through the space between the little fingers of the left hand, and interlace the thumb of the left hand through the space between the little fingers of the right hand. Slightly separate the six fingers of both hands so that they resemble a three-pronged vajra. This is the *samaya* hand-seal of the Vajra Family. These three seals are called the Great Seals (*mahāmudrā*).
Even the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cannot contravene this, let alone the various classes of Māras.

Each should, according to their own division, practice the methods of implementation in their proper sequence. This not only accords with the teachings, but also extinguishes all transgressions and eliminates all calamities; whatever Dharma one seeks shall surely fulfill one's aspirations.
Next, one should dispel the obstacles of the *vināyakas* within the body by means of mantras and mudrās.

The mantra is: "Oṃ amṛte hana hana hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra for dispelling the obstacles of the *vināyakas* within the body. As for the form of the mudrā: clench both hands into fists by bending the thumbs inside the palms; extend the two index fingers and interlace them left and right into the "tiger's mouth" (*vyāghramukha*). Move this mudrā from the crown of the head down to the feet and release it. This is the mudrā for dispelling the obstacles of the *vināyakas* and so forth.
Next, one should perform the ritual of expulsion using mantras and mudrās.

The mantra is as follows: *Namo vajraya hūṃ haṃ taṃ tuṃ maṃtra vighna-sucara hūṃ phaṭ*. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for expulsion. As for the form of the mudrā: bend the left thumb into the palm, press the middle and ring fingers down upon the thumb, bend the index finger against the side of the middle finger’s joint, and likewise bend the little finger against the side of the ring finger’s middle joint. Then, extend the arm and rotate it three times clockwise above the head, while touching the five points of the body with the mudrā.

Press the thumb of the right hand against the nail of the little finger, extend the remaining three fingers straight upward to form the shape of a *vajra*, and place it at the side of the waist; the ritual procedure is as before—this is the mudrā for expelling obstructors.
Furthermore, there are the mantras and mudrās for expelling obstructors.

The mantra is: "Oṃ vajratāra hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this three times; this is the mantra for expelling obstructors. As for the form of the mudrā: strike the palm of the left hand with the right hand in this manner three times; this is the mudrā for expelling obstructors.
Furthermore, there are the mantras and mudrās for warding off [obstacles].
The mantra is: "Oṃ kili kili rāvaḷadra hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra for warding off. As for the form of the mudrā: snap the fingers with both hands three times; this is the mudrā for warding off.
What is meant by "expelling" (vidhūnana)?
It refers to the act of banishing all obstacles from objects such as a shrine room, flowers, clothing, and seats; this is called expelling, through which one attains purity.
Next, the mantras and mudrās for the removal of impurities (*malotsarga*) are explained.

The mantra is: "Oṃ kili kili vajra hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for the removal of impurities. As for the characteristics of the mudrā: with the right hand, press the thumb upon the nail of the little finger, extend the remaining three fingers straight upward and slightly apart, and place them against the waist. With the three fingers pointing forward, perform the same gesture with the left hand. Use these to seal all objects to eliminate defilement and evil; this is called the *Malotsarga* mudrā of the Kīli-anger deity.

Next, perform the purification: using the *hṛdaya-mantra* of the Buddha Family, form a fist and take scented water; recite it seven times and sprinkle it upon all objects, whereby they become purified.
First, the Heart Mantra of the Buddha Family is:
"Oṃ jvala-jvālaya. Recite this seven times. The Heart Mantra of the Lotus Family is:
"Oṃ āloka. This is the Heart Mantra of the Lotus Family. The Heart Mantra of the Vajra Family is:
"Oṃ vajratilaka hūṃ. This is the heart-mantra of the Vajra Family. Next, to produce luster: by reciting the mantra and forming the mudrā, one seals all objects, whereby they become lustrous.
First, the mantra for radiance of the Buddha Family is:
"Oṃ te-te-ye ti-ti-śe vi-ne ti-te svā-dhā hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this three times; this is the radiance mantra of the Buddha Family.

The mantra for radiance of the Lotus Family is: "Oṃ ni-bi-ye ni-bi-ye ni-pa-ya mahā-śrī-ye svā-hā. Recite this three times; this is the radiance mantra of the Lotus Family. The mantra for radiance of the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ jvala jvālaya mantre svāhā. Recite this three times; this is the *jvālana-mantra* (Glossy Radiance Mantra) of the Vajra Family. As for the mudrā: with the left hand, place the thumb upon the nail of the little finger, and extend the remaining three fingers straight upward with slight gaps between them. Extend the arm, then form the same mudrā with the right hand, supporting the underside of the left elbow. By touching objects with this mudrā, they become glossy. This is used throughout the three families; it is the universal *jvālana-mudrā* (Glossy Radiance Mudrā) for the three families.

The *Susiddhikara-pūjā-vidhi*, Volume One (in the Danzang [Dunhuang] collection, it is titled the *Susiddhikara-sūtra*); since the titles differ and the text is also significantly different, yet the translator is the same.

Now, upon examining the scriptures of the Danzang (Tang Canon), this *Sūtra on the Method of Making Offerings* is entirely absent from the beginning to the end of both the Guo and Song editions. Although it does appear in the Gan-han (Box) of the Danzang, a detailed search of the two catalogs—the *Kaiyuan* and *Zhenyuan*—reveals that among the works translated by Śubhakarasiṃha, there are only three sūtras and one dharma, and this *Sūtra on the Method of Making Offerings* is not among them.

Although it is not included in the current catalog, a detailed examination of its textual meaning reveals that it was not compiled by later forgers; therefore, I have retained both versions according to the Danzang (Dunhuang Canon).

From the *Susiddhikara Sūtra: Rituals for Offerings*, Volume [Number], the Sequential Order of the Three Families, translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Next, the ritual for protecting the body: perform the hand-mudrā of the Vidyārāja and recite this mantra while sealing the crown of the head...
At these five locations, one’s body becomes firmly protected.
The mantra is: *Oṃ vajra-jñiṃ praṇipataye svāhā*. Recite this five times; this is the mantra for protecting the body.

As for the characteristics of this hand seal (*mudrā*): interlace the two little fingers within the palms; press the two ring fingers together upon the crossed little fingers, inserting them into the palms; place the tips of the two middle fingers upright and touching one another; press the two index fingers onto the middle joints of the two middle fingers, causing the middle joints of the index fingers to bend inward; and hold the two thumbs upright, resting against the middle fingers. This is the hand seal for protecting the body.
Next, perform the Great Protection of the Body (*mahārakṣā*). Recite this mantra and form the mudrā; likewise, [place it] on the five locations to achieve the Great Protection of the Body.

The mantra is: "Oṃ jvalanaye hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this five times; this is the mantra for the Great Protection of the Body. The characteristics of its mudrā are identical to the previously mentioned protection mudrā.
Next, one should don the armor by reciting the mantra and forming the mudrā, rubbing from the crown of the head down to the feet; thus, the donning of armor is accomplished. The mantra is:
“Oṃ dhuvi dhuvi kāya dhuvi prajvalini svāhā. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for donning the armor. As for the form of the mudrā, extend the fingers wide.
Next, using the mantra and mudrā, the mantra for binding the hair is as follows:

"Oṃ susiddhikari svāhā. This is the mantra for binding the hair, used for all three families. As for the form of the mudrā: form a fist with the right hand and extend the thumb straight upward, placing it upon the crown of the head; this is the mudrā for binding the hair, used for all three families.
Furthermore, the hair-binding mantra of the Buddha Family is as follows:
"Namaḥ samantāya te vigatasaṃsārātmane oṃ susiddhalocane svāhā. Recite this seven times; this is the hair-binding mantra of the Buddha Family.

The hair-binding mantra of the Lotus Family is as follows: "Namo ratnatrayāya namaḥ padmanarteśvaryai oṃ khaṭe svāhā. Recite this seven times; this is the hair-binding mantra of the Lotus Family. The hair-binding mantra of the Vajra Family is as follows:

"Namo ratnatrayāya, namo śrīvajrapāṇaye, mahāyakṣasenāpataye, namaḥ kālakarṇa-dāruṇi ucchvāsani-kṣveḍa-śāntike karikaṭani kaṭani pātaya svāhā. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for binding the hair of the Vajra Family. The form of its mudrā is the same as the previous one.

Regarding the placement of the precious throne: whichever direction the principal deity happens to face first, one should next visualize a great ocean in that place. Upon that ocean, visualize a mountain of jewels; at its summit, visualize a lion throne. Above that, there is a subtle and wondrous great lotus pedestal, and above that, one should further contemplate various jeweled pavilions adorned with hanging silk banners, parasols, victory banners, and jeweled nets.

Having visualized the mental image, one subsequently recites the mantra; by adding this to what was previously visualized, each and every thing is accomplished, which is called the "Ocean of Accomplishment.
The mantra is: *Oṃ abhimāruṇadhe hūṃ*. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for the Ocean of Accomplishment. Next, the mantra for accomplishing the lion throne is taught:
"Oṃ acara hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this three times. Next, the mantra for accomplishing the Jewel Mountain is taught:
"Oṃ acara vīja svāhā. Recite this three times. Next, the mantra for accomplishing the Lotus is taught:
"Oṃ kamaḷa svāhā. Recite this three times. Next, the mantra for accomplishing the various adornments such as the Jewel Pavilion is taught:
"Oṃ namo sarvatathāgatānāṃ sarvatathāgatodgate svapraheśvara-maheśvara-gaganaketa svāhā. Recite this three times; this is...
Regarding the offering of *argha* water with the "Mantra for Accomplishing the Jewel Pavilion":
one should prepare a vessel according to the specific class (*kula*) and the requirements for the accomplishment of the rite— namely, a vessel made of gold,
silver, refined copper, stone, wood, earthenware, *śaṅkha*, or *kocī* (a tree known in the local language as *pācī*).
Using leaves such as lotus petals and the like—one must ensure they are not broken, deficient, coarse, rough, or perforated—fill them completely with scented water.
Arrange various flowers according to their respective families (kula) and their superior, middling, or inferior quality.
Recite the *karmakara-mantra* (action mantra), and further recite the *kulamātṛ-mantras* (family mother mantras) and others; then, recite over the *argha* water.
Place [the implements] on the left side.
The mantras and mudrās for performing the rites are those previously explained, such as the mantras and mudrās for warding off obstacles and so forth.
Next, the mantras and mudrās of the Family Mothers (Kulamātṛs) and others will be explained.
First, the mantra of the Mother of the Buddha Family is recited as follows:

"Namaḥ prajñāpāramitāyai | oṃ lū lū sarvārthasiddhini svāhā. This is the mantra of the Mother of the Buddha Family; she is Buddhalocanā. It is to be recited three times. Next, the mantra of the Mother of the Lotus Family is as follows:

*Naraśaṃ saṃvaraśaṃ bhe viśrava-maṃrāṇe caśamaṃ haṃ sarvasattvānāṃ sarvavidyādhipataye svāhā.* Recite this three times. This is the mantra of the Lotus Family (*padmakula*); its name is *Bhaṇḍaravasinī*. The mantra of the Mother of the Vajra Family (*vajrakulamātṛ*) is as follows:

"Oṃ āḥ mūlavidyāratnaya namaḥ śrīvajrapāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpataye oṃ kulanandari bandha phaṭ. Recite this three times; this is the mantra of the Mother of the Vajra Family, which is Mañjuśrī. Next, the Family Heart Mantra is taught.
The heart mantra of the first, the Buddha Family, is:
"Oṃ īraṇīrka. Recite this seven times. The heart mantra of the Lotus Family is:
"Oṃ ālulika. Recite this seven times. The heart mantra of the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ vajratr̥ṣṭika. Recite this seven times. Next, the mudrā of Buddhalocanā, the Mother of the Buddha Family, is explained: join both hands together; bend the two thumbs and insert them simultaneously into the palms; place them straight against the middle joints of the two middle fingers without bending those joints; slightly bend the index fingers so that they press down upon the backs of the upper joints of the two middle fingers—this is the characteristic of the Buddha-root mudrā.

Next, the hand-seal (mudrā) of the Mother of the Lotus Family is described: join the palms; bend all ten fingers together so that their tips touch, leaving the center of the palms hollow like an unopened lotus flower, while keeping the wrists joined. This is the *ardhaparyaṅka* hand-seal of Padmamātā.

Next, the mudrā of Vajravārāhī of the Vajra Family is described: join the palms; bend the two index fingers and the two ring fingers so they enter into the palms with their backs touching each other; the remaining six fingers are held straight and upright, touching one another. This is the mudrā of Vajravārāhī.

It is further stated that one may also join the palms and bend the two index fingers and the two ring fingers, crossing them so that they face outward; pressing the joints with the right finger over the left, while the remaining six fingers are held upright and touching one another—this, too, is correct.
Next, the mudrās for the heart-mantras of the families are explained.

First, the heart-mudrā of the Buddha Family: interlace the eight fingers and insert them into the palms so that the middle joints of the eight fingers are exposed; extend the two thumbs straight upward without touching the index fingers, maintaining a distance of half an inch. This is the heart-mudrā of the Buddha Family.

Next, the hand gestures (mudrās) of the heart of the Lotus Family are explained. Following the heart gesture of the Buddha Family, one merely changes it by bending the right thumb into the palm and holding the left thumb upright; this is the Vajra Heart Gesture.
Regarding the method for the argha offering, it should be performed according to the specific family (kula) and the accomplishment of the rite, as explained extensively in the teachings.
At the time of presentation, one should offer it while reciting the root mantra.

Having invited the Principal Deity, the practitioner, while performing the ritual at the designated site, first visualizes the deity already seated; next, by means of mantras and mudrās, they accomplish the celestial chariot and escort the deity to his abode.

The mantra for the chariot is: "Oṃ tūru tūru hūṃ. This is the general mantra for sending forth the chariot common to the three families. As for the mudrā: interlace the six fingers below the middle fingers of both hands, placing the right over the left and inserting them into the palms. Join the two index fingers together, and place the two thumbs alongside the sides of the middle fingers. Open the two palms slightly so that the wrists touch and the six fingers are joined at their bases; this is the mudrā for sending forth the chariot common to the three families.

Once the ritual vehicles have been sent forth, one should immediately recite this mantra, inserting the phrase for the arrival [of the deity], while forming the mudrā; one may either invoke the principal deity alone or summon both the deity and their retinue.

When sending [the deities] away, move the left thumb outward and raise it; when welcoming them, move the right thumb inward and bend it. Perform this three times each for both the outward and inward movements.

The mantra is: *Oṃ va-ra-ṇi-ka-ra-sa-svāhā*. This is the general mantra for inviting the deities of the three families. Following this mantra, one should place the phrase for welcoming, which may be understood according to the previous instructions.

Regarding the mudrā: it follows the previous chariot-mudrā, with the sole modification that the tip of the right thumb is joined to the tip of the left middle finger; this is the general invocation mudrā for the three families.
Alternatively, one may place the word for "coming" (*āgaccha*) within the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra), which is then called the heart-mantra.
Next, one places *e e he bhagavan*. Following that, one knows the mantra for welcoming from the heart-mantra itself; then, one performs the mudrā with the hands and issues the invitation.
If one invokes the Honored One with the Family Heart Mantra, He will joyfully come swiftly.
First, the Family Heart Mantra of the Buddha Family is:

"Oṃ īraṇe" (recite this twenty-five times). As for the mudrā: following the previous Family Heart Mudrā, change only by pointing the two thumbs forward; beckoning three times constitutes the Invitation Mudrā. This is the Invitation Mudrā of the Buddha Family.
The heart mantra of the Lotus Family is:

"Oṃ āḥ rucika. Recite this five times. As for the mudrā, follow the heart mudrā of the preceding family, with the sole modification that the right thumb is extended forward; reciting it three times accomplishes the invocation. This is the invocation of the Lotus Family.
The heart mantra of the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ vajratrakka" (recite five times). As for the form of its mudrā, it follows the heart mudrā of the preceding family, with the sole modification that the left thumb is extended forward and beckoned; after three recitations, this becomes the invitation mudrā. This is the invitation mudrā of the Vajra Family.
When one wishes to perform the invitation (*āvāhana*), first take hold of an incense burner and recite the mantra to purify the path within the chamber, and only then perform the invitation.
The mantra for purification is:

*Oṃ susiddhikari jvalitadīpanatha mulidaye jvala jvala bandha hana hana hūṃ phaṭ*. This is the mantra for purifying the path belonging to the Vajra Family; it is also called [the mantra] of two families. The mantra for purifying the path belonging to the Buddha Family is as follows:
“Oṃ jvala. This is the mantra for purifying the path belonging to the Buddha Family.

The mantra for purifying the path belonging to the Lotus Family is: “Oṃ padmanīṃ vagati mughe mughe nāgani svāhā. This is the mantra for purifying the path belonging to the Lotus Family. Having performed this rite, all the locks within the chamber shall be opened; it also accomplishes the expulsion [of obstacles] up to purification, as well as the awakening of the tutelary deity.
First, one should perform the mantra for the invitation (*āhvāna*). Its phrases are as follows:

*Īkṣe he he bhagavan namo 'stu te jaya jaya svāhā*. This is the general mantra for the phrases of invitation common to the three families, which has already been explained previously. One should invite the Honored One by assuming a posture corresponding to that deity’s specific seat, its signs of joy and so forth, and even its way of looking toward the practitioner, manifesting those very forms and characteristics.

Regarding the expulsion of those belonging to Māra: there is a *vināyaka* named "Sender of the Honored Ones" (*saṃpreṣaṇa*) who invites the Honored Ones; one should immediately expel him using the *kīli kīli* mantra and its corresponding mudrā.

The mantra is: "Oṃ kili kili vajra hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times; this is the *kili-kili* mantra. As for the mudrā: with the left hand, press the thumb against the nail of the little finger, extend the three remaining fingers, and form the shape of a *vajra*, holding it outward. This is the *kili-kili-vajra-mudrā*, which is used for expulsion.

Regarding "observing the *samaya*": once the honored one has been escorted away and the *vināyaka*s are about to depart, the principal deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) intends to follow them; therefore, one observes the *samaya* to cause them to remain and not depart.
At that time, one should gaze with the right hand while reciting this mantra to cause [the deity] to remain, thereby causing the tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā) to remember its original vow.

The mantra is: "Oṃ vaimacchare samaya svāhā. Recite it seven times; this is the Samaya-gazing mantra. As for the hand gesture (mudrā): with the right hand, press the thumb against the nail of the little finger, extend the three fingers to form the shape of a vajra, and point it outward. This is the Kili-kili Vajra-mudrā, which is used for gazing.

Regarding the offering of a seat and requesting [the deity] to sit: first, having bound the inner boundary (*antarmāṇḍala*) with vajra-kīlas and so forth in the designated area and above it, one should immediately offer *argha* water and then request [the deity] to be seated.

One should offer arghya by reciting its own specific mantra, or alternatively, by reciting the general arghya mantra. According to the distinctions of the *sādhana* and the *kriyā-tantra*, one should hold the arghya vessel and place it at the heart and so forth, even down to prostrating on the knees while making the offering—namely, for the three families, one offers it at the forehead; for the celestial family (*deva-kula*), one offers it at the heart; and for the terrestrial family (*bhūmi-kula*), one offers it at the knees.

The mantra is: *Oṃ bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabhāya pūjāyai pūja svāhā*. This is the general mantra and mudrā for reciting over the argha vessel. At dawn, at midday, and at sunset—during these three times—one should offer the lotus seat with this mantra and mudrā.
The mantra of the Buddha Family is: "Oṃ vīra vīraya svāhā. This is the seat-offering mantra of the Buddha Family. The mantra of the Lotus Family is:
"Oṃ bhañja vīraya svāhā. This is the seat-offering mantra of the Lotus Family. The mantra of the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ vajravīryā svāhā. This is the mantra for offering the seat in the Vajra Family. As for the mudrā: join the two hands in *añjali*; place the index, middle, and ring fingers together and slightly apart within the palms at a distance of about four finger-widths; keep the thumbs and both little fingers touching and held upright. This is the general mudrā for offering the lotus in all three families.

If one prepares garments, necklaces, and so forth, and performs the rite of offering them after reciting the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-mantra*, one should bind the boundary of the ground using the *vajra-kīla* method and bind the upper direction using the *vajra-sthālī* method.

The mantra for the Vajra Stake is: “Oṃ kili kili vajravajri bhura bhandha bhandha hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this Vajra Stake mantra three times. As for the mudrā: extend the left middle and ring fingers outward and insert them between the right middle and ring fingers. Twist the left ring finger around the right ring finger; join the tips of the two little fingers, the tips of the two thumbs, and the tips of the two index fingers, which are held straight up. Using this seal, extend both arms as wings so that the tips of the two thumbs touch the ground, and while reciting the mantra, bind the boundary of the earth. This is the Vajra Stake mudrā.
Next, use the Vajra-Railing mantra and mudrā to bind the boundary above.

The mantra is: "Oṃ viśvara nara kṣava-jra-pañjara hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this three times; this is the Vajra-Railing mantra. As for the form of the mudrā, it follows the previous pillar-mudrā, with the exception that the two thumbs are placed flat against the sides of the two index fingers. Raising the mudrā upward while reciting the mantra constitutes the binding of the space-boundary; this is the Vajra-Railing mudrā.
One forms the vajra-brazier using the Vajra-brazier mantra and mudrā. The mantra is: "Oṃ sara sara vajraprakara hūṃ phaṭ.

This is the Vajra-brazier mantra. As for the characteristics of its mudrā: based on the previous *kīla* (stake) mudrā, one changes only the two thumbs, which are spread apart and held upright. One performs three clockwise circumambulations from the south while reciting this mantra; thus the Vajra-brazier is accomplished. This is the ritual method for the Vajra-brazier mudrā; it is said that what precedes this constitutes the internal characteristics within the triple world.
Next, one binds the boundary of the eastern direction with the Vajrapāśa mantra and mudrā.

The mantra is: "Oṃ vajrapāśahṛdaya gagaṇamāla hūṃ. Recite this three times; this is the Vajrapāśa mantra. As for the form of the mudrā: bend the index finger of the left hand against the base of the thumb, and with the thumb held straight up, press down on the nail of the index finger, leaving a slight opening. The remaining three fingers are pressed together and held straight up. The right hand is likewise positioned, with the backs of its three fingers placed against the inner side of the three fingers of the left hand. This is the Vajrapāśa mudrā, used to bind the boundary of the eastern direction.
Next, one should bind the boundary of the western direction using the Vajrapatāka mantra and hand-seal method.
The mantra is: "Oṃ padma jñiṅ raṭa.

Recite this three times; this is the Vajrapatāka mantra. As for the form of the hand-seal: make a fist with the left hand, extend the thumb straight up, and place the five fingers of the right hand sideways upon the tip of the left thumb, with the palm facing the body. This is the Vajrapatāka seal-fist; the right hand is the same as the left, forming this same seal.
Next, one binds the northern boundary with the Vajrakali mantra and mudrā.

The mantra is: "Oṃ vajrakali raṭa maṭa. Recite this three times; this is the Vajrakali mantra. As for the characteristics of the mudrā: join the tips of the thumbs and little fingers of both hands together. Bend the remaining six fingers individually toward the palms, ensuring that the backs of the fingers do not touch one another, nor do they touch the palms. This is the Vajrakali mudrā for binding the northern boundary.
Next, one should bind the southern boundary using the Vajraśṛṅkhalā mantra and mudrā. The mantra is: "Oṃ vajraśṛṅkhalā ṭhaḥ maṭha.

Recite this three times; this is the Vajraśṛṅkhalā mantra. As for the characteristics of the mudrā: form a fist with the left hand and extend the thumb straight up. With the right hand, join the tips of the thumb and index finger, letting the tip of the thumb protrude slightly. Place the lower side of the right hand upon the tip of the left thumb, keeping the right thumb extended straight up. This is the Vajraśṛṅkhalā mudrā used to bind the southern boundary.
Next, recite the mantra seven times over the palm of the right hand and point with the fingers to bind the lower boundary (*adhaḥ-sīmā*).

The mantra is: "Oṃ śaṅkare svāhā. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for binding the lower boundary, though three recitations are also permissible. Next, using the Āsmaṇi mantra and its corresponding mudrā, universally establish the fire enclosure (*agni-koṭa*).

The mantra is: "Oṃ āsanagihini. Recite this three times with a nasalized sound (*phaṭ*). This is the *āsanagihini* mantra. As for the mudrā: place the back of the right hand inside the left hand so that there is no gap between them; extend both thumbs upward and straight. Rotate [the hands] once to the right, and the fire enclosure is formed. This is the *āsanagihini* mudrā.
Next, one should re-establish the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) by means of mantras and mudrās.

The mantra is: "Oṃ śaṅkare mahāśame svāhā. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for establishing the Great Boundary. As for the form of the mudrā: interlace the little fingers and ring fingers of both hands, inserting them into the palms. Straighten and erect the two middle fingers so that their tips touch. Bend the two index fingers over the second phalanges on the backs of the middle fingers, ensuring they do not touch the middle fingers, forming the shape of a three-pronged vajra. Place the two thumbs beside the index fingers. Rotate [the hands] throughout the eight directions, above, and below while reciting and maintaining the mantra; thus the Great Boundary is established. This is the mudrā for establishing the Great Boundary.

Having performed this, even if those near the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin or other practitioners of discordant mantras should attempt to cause harm, they will be unable to do so; nor can they diminish the majestic power of the tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā). Furthermore, all those who employ spells for breaking [obstacles], binding with *kheṭaka*, or casting off afflictions shall find no opportunity to prevail.

Regarding "equipping with vajras, etc.": one should not purify the various vajras, rosaries, rings, waist-bands, sacred threads (*brahmasūtra*), armlets, lotuses, banners, and so forth with scented water or other substances; rather, one should hold and recite them while employing the mantra of the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). During both the time of recitation (*japa*) and the fire sacrifice (*homa*), all such items as these must be fully prepared.

Next, the methods for accomplishing other objects such as the vajra are explained. As for the vajra, it should be placed within a vessel according to its appropriate correspondence and installed upon a seat before oneself, having been anointed with red sandalwood incense.

Next, holding incense, flowers, and other offerings, one should invite the Lord of Mantras; by reciting that mantra while offering the incense and flowers, and further reciting it one thousand times, it is called "accomplishment."
The mantra of Vajra is: "Oṃ duna vajra hā.
This is the mantra for accomplishing Vajra. One should fashion a three-pronged vajra from red sandalwood or similar materials and perform one thousand recitations.
Next, the mantra for purifying the rosary of the Buddha Family is stated as follows:
"Namo ratnatrayāya oṃ ānate viśuddhe siddhisiddhārthe svāhā. This is the mantra for purifying the rosary of the Buddha Family.

The mantra for the rosary of the Lotus Family is as follows: "Namo bhagavatyai oṃ amṛtendrakīle śrīmālini svāhā. This is the mantra for purifying the rosary of the Lotus Family. The mantra for purifying the rosary of the Vajra Family is as follows:

*Namo ratnatrayāya namaḥ śrīvajrapāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpataye | oṃ kili kili laucini svāhā.* This is the mantra for purifying the rosary of the Vajra family. Using these respective mantras for purifying the rosaries of the three families, one should thread the beads through their holes while reciting the specific mantra of each family seven times for every single bead. Once the threading and tying are complete, one should again recite the mantra one hundred times. Furthermore, one should purify the rosary according to the previous method and perform the accomplishment (*sādhana*) using this mantra.
The mantra for accomplishing the rosary in the Buddha Family is:
*Oṃ namo bhagavatyai siddhisādhyasiddhārthe svāhā*. This is the mantra for accomplishing the rosary in the Buddha Family.

The mantra for accomplishing the rosary in the Lotus Family is: *Oṃ vaśumatiśrīye padmamālini svāhā*. This is the mantra for accomplishing the rosary in the Lotus Family. The mantra for accomplishing the rosary in the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ vajrīrtanaye svāhā. This is the mantra for the accomplishment of the rosary of the Vajra Family. Using this mantra for the accomplishment of the rosary, one should invoke the mantra of that particular family upon the rosary; furthermore, at the time of making offerings, one should recite it one thousand times to achieve accomplishment.

Next, the characteristics of the hand-mudrā for holding the rosary are explained: with the right hand, press the tip of the ring finger with the thumb, extend the middle finger straight, slightly bend the little finger, and place the index finger against the side of the middle phalanx of the middle finger; this is the rosary-holding mudrā common to the three families.

Next, the mudrā for holding the rosary in the Lotus Family is described: with the right hand, press the tip of the middle finger with the thumb, and extend the remaining three fingers straight; do the same with the left hand. This is the mudrā for holding the rosary in the Lotus Family.

Next, the mudrā for holding the rosary in the Vajra family is described: form a fist with the right hand, extend the thumb straight, and press it against the index finger; do the same with the left hand. This is the mudrā for holding the rosary in the Vajra family.
One should use *akṣa* seeds for the Buddha family as a rosary, lotus seeds for the Mañjuśrī (Padma) family as a rosary, and *rudrākṣa* seeds for the Vajra family as a rosary.

Furthermore, it is said that one may take the seeds of the living son-tree (*jīvaputra*), the lotus-seed (*padmabīja*), the *rudrākṣa*, the conch-shell (*śaṅkha*), or stones, wood, *naktamāla* seeds, lead, tin, refined copper, or lapis lazuli; taking any one of these, one should fashion a rosary of more than a hundred beads. Holding it with the right hand and with an undistracted mind, once the recitation of the mantra is completed, one should count the beads all at once, ensuring there is no sequence of before and after.

Next, the method for the armlet is explained: within the armlet, one should thread a bead made from the heart of a living child or similar substance. One should then recite the mantra and perform the mudrā of the Family Mother (Kulīśvarī), making offerings of incense and flowers and sprinkling scented water. Finally, using this same mantra and mudrā of the Family Mother, one should invoke her presence and empower the armlet.

Furthermore, one should perform offerings in sequence with the *mudrā* and mantra of the Family Mother (*kulamātṛ*), reciting them up to one thousand times. Then, fashioning a ring from *nāba* grass and placing it on the ring finger, one accomplishes the rite as previously described using the Family Heart Mantra (*kulahr̥daya-mantra*), reciting it up to one thousand times for each respective family.

One should know the method for the waist-band in due order: have a young girl twist and join it together, dye it with kuṣṭha—here meaning red-blue flower or saffron—and accomplish it according to the previous rite, up to reciting the mantra one thousand times. When tied around the waist during recitation, during homa, or while sleeping, it will prevent the loss of semen.
The mantra for accomplishing the waistline is:
"Oṃ ara ara bandhani kṣiprakrīḍāraṇi siddhārthike svāhā. From the *Susiddhikara-pūjā-vidhi*, Middle Volume;
[and] *Susiddhikara-pūjā-vidhi*, Lower Volume.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty:
Within the Buddha Family, the thread is white; within the Lotus Family, the thread is yellow;
and within the Vajra Family, the thread is red. Only when these items are fully prepared upon one's person may the ritual be performed.

Relying on the sūtras and the classes [of tantras], once the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) has been established as described in the sūtras, one should next perform the offerings. According to the specific accomplishments and the distinctions of the ritual class (*kriyā-tantra*), one should prepare unguents whose color, taste, and fragrance correspond to those [deities]. Having recited this mantra and the root mantra over the previously poured-off impurities up to the lustrous unguents, one should then form the hand gestures (*mudrā*) and present them as an offering.
The mantra for offering scented unguent (*vilepana*) is as follows:
*Īśānamayaṃ vāsudevaṃ niviśeṣu yaśo yaśoyujaṃ mañjanīve nidhuvakṣitipratigṛhya pragṛhṇāmi | Oṃ ahara ahara sara vaviniyadrapūrti svāhā.* Recite this seven times;
this is the mantra for the offering of scented unguent.
"It is employed for all three families. As for the form of the hand seal (*mudrā*),
extend the five fingers of the right hand with the palm facing outward.
With the left hand facing upward, grasp the four fingers of the right wrist with the thumb on the inside;
this is the mudrā for offering scented ointment (*gandha*).
This is to be employed for all three families.
Furthermore, the mantra for offering scented unguent (*vilepana*) to the Buddha Family is:

"Oṃ akṣatarāgraviśaye namaḥ svāhā. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for offering scented unguent to the Buddha Family. The mantra for offering scented unguent to the Lotus Family is as follows:

"Oṃ nṛti nṛtya nṛttapate nṛtyāpate hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for offering scented unguents (*vilepana*) to the Lotus Family (*padmakula*). The mantra for offering scented unguents to the Vajra Family (*vajrakula*) is:

"Oṃ visara visara hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for offering scented unguents to the Vajra Family. Recite these mantras, as well as the primary mantras, over the previously offered impurities up to the luster, and likewise over the flowers. Then, forming the appropriate hand gestures (*mudrā*), offer them.
The mantra for offering flowers is as follows:

*Īṣe svamānani viye śuśre śuśre yunāñce nāmañje veṇita bakṭiye pratti-ghrihe prasanname oṃ āhara āhara sarvaviyadara-pūrite svāhā*. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for offering flowers, used for all three families (*trikula*). As for the mudrā, it is like the carriage-wheel mudrā, with the exception that the two index fingers are crossed; this is the flower-offering mudrā, used for all three families.
Furthermore, the mantra for offering flowers to the Buddha Family is:
“Oṃ śigye śike svāhā. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for offering flowers to the Buddha Family. The mantra for offering flowers to the Lotus Family is:
“Oṃ caṇiṃ gandhamudraṇe hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for offering flowers to the Lotus Family. The mantra for offering flowers to the Vajra Family is:

Recite "Oṃ bhrūṃ jvalanta svāhā" seven times; this is the mantra for offering flowers to the Vajra Family. Then, for the impurities that were previously poured out, up to the luster, burn the incense while reciting this mantra as well as the root mantra, and further perform the hand gestures (*mudrā*) to present them.
The mantra for offering incense is as follows:

"Akṣobhyavanditara-suhṛdīya-kalyāṇagandha-udbhūta-surabhau jvalan-mayane vande tvām bhaktyā nivedayāmi bhoḥ kṛtin yathābhipretaṃ pratigṛhṇīṣva | Oṃ ahara hara sarvavidyādharapūjite svāhā. Recite this seven times.
"This is the mantra for offering incense,
which is used in common for all three families. As for the mudrā,
join the little fingers, ring fingers, and middle fingers of both hands, bending them inward together.
Place the backs of the two index fingers touching,
pointing upward and held straight; their sides face each other, separated by the distance of one barley grain.
Place the two thumbs broadside against the sides of the two index fingers; this is the mantra for offering incense, used throughout the three families.
Furthermore, the mantra for offering incense in the Buddha Family is as follows:
Recite seven times: “Namo kṣetramantraviseṣaye śrīṅ svāhā. The mantra for burning incense in the Lotus Family (*padmakula*) is:

“Oṃ caṇḍarabhaṇḍaligalanajini hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for burning incense in the Lotus Family. The mantra for offering burning incense in the Vajra Family (*vajrakula*) is: “Oṃ visara sara hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times.

Next, regarding the previously poured-out impurities up to the luster, one should empower the food and drink with this mantra as well as their respective root mantras, and then offer them while forming the appropriate hand gestures (*mudrā*).
The mantra for offering food is as follows:

*Vauṣaṭ tīrṇa-rāśe hṛdaya-harṣa-eṣāṃ pūrṇatara-syān-mālyam | etāni satkārāhārāṇi bhaktyā niryātayāmi tubhyaṃ durbhikṣe pratisare he prākṣaṇāme || Oṃ ahara ahara sarvavinyadarabūrdhe svāhā.* Recite this seven times.
"This is for the offering of food, to be used throughout the three families. As for the mudrā:
turn both hands upward with the two palms facing forward and touching side by side.
The sides of the tips of the two ring fingers are joined and slightly bent;
the tips of the two index fingers are pressed against the sides of the middle fingers.
Place the two thumbs side-by-side against the sides of the two index fingers,
resembling the gesture of cupping water; this is the *bhojana-dāna-mudrā* (offering-food seal),
used throughout the three families.
Furthermore, the mantra for offering food to the Buddha Family is:
"Oṃ cchreṇi ni svāhā. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for offering food to the Buddha Family.

The mantra for offering food to the Lotus Family is: "Oṃ jvalu kiṇi svāhā. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for offering food to the Middle Family (Lotus Family). The mantra for offering food to the Vajra Family is:

"Recite 'Oṃ vajriṇi vajra-ārye svāhā' seven times; this is the mantra for offering food to the lower [deities]. Furthermore, one should pour away impurities until [the vessel] has a lustrous appearance, then offer it by reciting this mantra and the root mantra while performing the hand gestures (mudrā)."
The mantra of Dīpaṃkara is as follows:
"Rakṣa rakṣa | Protect, protect! You who are pure and capable of removing ignorance;
through these offerings made with devotion, I pray that you graciously accept them."
traḥ kṣetra-dhūmaviṭaṃ maṅgala-śubha-maṅgiṇi venidu-bhaktiye nīpāyana-pratigṛhyatām | oṃ ālokaya lokaya saḥ ||
Recite "Rāva-vindita-dhara-pūrite svāhā" seven times;
this is the mantra for offering lamps, to be used for all three families. As for the mudrā:
form a fist with the right hand, extend the middle finger, and hold its tip straight upward; this is the lamp-offering mudrā.
This is to be employed for all three families (*kula*).
Furthermore, the mantra for offering lamps to the Buddha Family is as follows:
"Oṃ amaro-udbhūti-tejini svāhā. Recite this three times; this is the mantra for offering lamps to the Buddha Family. The mantra for offering lamps to the Central Family is as follows:

"Oṃ jvālini jvāla-jvalana-kṛta phaṭ. Recite this three times; this is the mantra for offering lamps to the middle [section]. The mantra for offering lamps to the lower [section] is: "Oṃ vimala-dhūpa-caraṇa hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this three times;

this is the mantra for offering lamps to the lower [section]. Regarding the mental offering performed with mantras and mudrās: even if one is unable to provide offerings such as scented unguents up to the lamp-light, by merely reciting the aforementioned mantras for offering scented unguents and so forth and performing the mudrās, the complete offering is accomplished.

Next, regarding making offerings by means of mental visualization: one employs the mind to imagine that all manner of flowers from both water and land, unowned and unappropriated, fill the entirety of space throughout the ten directions;
likewise, one visualizes clouds of exquisite unguents for humans and devas, along with incense, lamps, banners, pennants, parasols, various musical instruments, songs, dances, and performances.
...pearl nets, suspended jeweled bells, flower garlands, white whisks, exquisite gongs and chimes, *kiṅkiṇī* nets,
wish-fulfilling jewel trees, clouds of celestial garments, various celestial foods of supreme fragrance and flavor,
and various pavilions adorned with precious pillars; [and] the celestial ornaments for the head...

Clouds of crowns, necklaces, and so forth— when the practitioner directs their mind so that these fill the entirety of space and makes such offerings with a heart of utmost sincerity, this is the most supreme form of worship.

The practitioner who undertakes this with a resolute mind performs this rite; by directing the mind toward making offerings, reciting this mantra, and forming mudrās, all the aforementioned visualized offerings will be fully accomplished.

The mantra is: "Oṃ sarvatathāgatodbhavatejasaṃbhara he maṅga gaṇa jvaṃ svāhā. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for the accomplishment of the mental offering. As for the mudrā: interlace the two hands in the añjali gesture, with the right hand pressing over the left, and place it upon the crown of the head. This is the mudrā for the accomplishment of the mental offering.

In performing any offering, one should possess this method: with utmost sincerity and faith, and while presenting argha water, one should accomplish it through the recitation of mantras and mudrās; furthermore, by directing the mind and joining the palms, placing them upon the crown of the head, the rite of perfect offering is thereby completed.

Regarding one’s own seat: one should prepare a seat from *nāba* grass or other types of grass, measuring sixteen finger-widths in length, four finger-widths in thickness, and twelve finger-widths in width; one should sit upon it in accordance with the specific requirements of the accomplishment and the particular ritual.
Regarding the methods of sitting, there are briefly three types:
first, the full lotus posture (paryaṅka); second, the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka); and third, the bhadrāsana. One should keep the body upright and motionless while performing the recitation.

Holding the rosary with the hand mudrā and placing it before one's heart, perform the recitation; first pay homage to the Triple Gem, next pay homage to the primary deity (iṣṭadevatā), and then universally pay homage to all other honored ones before performing the recitation.

At the outset, one should first observe the deity for a brief moment and then perform the recitation. During the interval, do not give rise to various unwholesome discriminations, such as anger or attachment; maintain right mindfulness while reciting and holding the mantra, visualizing the form of the deity, or visualizing the letters of the mantra, or sometimes visualizing the mantra letters upon the heart of that deity, or perform the recitation with a tranquil and pure mind.

Regarding the method of recitation: it should be neither too hurried nor too slow, neither too loud nor too faint. One must not converse with others during the interval, nor allow the mind to dwell on external objects. The syllables of the mantra must not be corrupted or mistaken. One should visualize the deity as if standing before one's eyes. During the two periods of morning and evening, the required number of recitations must be fully completed; at midday, the count should be reduced by half, or even further.
Within mantras, those containing the syllable *oṃ* and the word of homage (*namas*) should be recited with a tranquil mind;
if performing rites of pacification (*śāntika*) or enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), they should be recited in a low voice;
if the mantra contains the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, they should be recited with fierce anger.
If one performs [the rite] for the purpose of harming others, one should ensure that other people hear it while reciting.
Generally, regarding the number of syllables in a mantra: for those from one to four syllables, one should recite them until the count reaches ten million (koṭi) times;
for those from five to fifteen syllables, each individual syllable should be recited one hundred thousand (lakṣa) times.
If the text consists of fifteen to thirty-two characters, recite it three *lakṣas*;
if it exceeds this number, recite it ten thousand times.
Reciting according to the ritual at each session, once the count is completed, one should earnestly seek the fulfillment of whatever vows one harbors and the attainment of accomplishments (*siddhi*).

Regarding the protection of the root deity: within the Buddha Family, one should protect the yet-to-be-determined root deity with the Buddhalocanā mantra; within the Middle Family, one should protect the root deity with the Pāṇḍaravāsinī mantra; and within the Lower Family, one should protect the root deity with the Māmakī mantra.
At the initial moment of wishing to recite and at the moment of concluding the recitation—one should protect the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) during these two times.

If the mantra being recited is peaceful (*śāntika*), one should protect the *iṣṭadevatā* with a wrathful (*tāntrika*) mantra, or otherwise protect the *iṣṭadevatā* by means of the Lord of the Family (*kuleśvara*).
If the mantra being recited is wrathful, one should protect the *iṣṭadevatā* with a peaceful mantra, or otherwise protect the *iṣṭadevatā* by means of the Lord of the Family.
If one feels joy while reciting the mantra, one should protect the deity with both peaceful and wrathful mantras. Regarding the dedication of merit:
once the recitation is finished, one should protect the number of recitations with the Family Mother (Kulīśvarī) and entrust them to the Lord of the Family.
It should be understood that one speaks thus:

"All sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance; they seek only to receive and believe in Bodhi. I now do this for their sake, not for my own. I only pray that when the World-Honored One achieves it, you will return the count to me."
Having completed the recitation, next hold the argha vessel at the crown of your head and offer it.

Again, perform worship with incense, flowers, and other offerings to form the samaya bond; again perform the protection of the Dharma, having the Family Mother protect the principal deity, and likewise protect yourself with the Family Mother or the Vidyārāja. Form the āsanga-ñiṅ mudrā and recite its mantra.

Rotate the mudrā to the left; all protections previously established are thereby completely released. The form of the hand-mudrā is the same as the Invitation Mudrā, with the sole modification that the two thumbs are extended outward, which constitutes the dismissal. Within the mantra of invitation, add the phrase "Go, go" (gaccha gaccha), and it becomes the mantra of dismissal.

Regarding the section on *homa*: as in the sequence for recitation, all procedures for *homa*, ritual bathing, and even the invitation of the *iṣṭadevatā* (principal deity) are identical to the rules for recitation.

The wood for the homa fuel consists of: udumbara wood, aśvattha wood, nyagrodha wood, lakṣanyagrodha wood, maṅgala wood, aśoka wood, śrīparṇī wood, nyagrodha wood, āmra wood, khadira wood, śamī wood, plakṣa wood, apāmārga wood, mandūka wood, jīmūtaka wood, and so forth.

Taking wood of this kind, cut it to the length of ten fingers; dip both ends into milk, clarified butter, curd, and honey, and perform homa for all rites of accomplishment, as well as for pacifying, increasing, and harming others.
The materials for the homa are as follows: lotus flowers, curd-rice, ghee and milk, sesame seeds, honey, mustard seeds, salt, and so forth.

One should place the hearth between the principal deity and oneself; it should be one cubit square and half a cubit deep, or it may be circular. It should be constructed either indoors or outdoors, ensuring that it is visible to the deity, and prepared according to the ritual rules.

On all four sides, install steps with a rim placed around the mouth of the fire-pit; these should measure four finger-widths in height. Within the pit, place a wheel, and the other various objects and seals should each be one finger-width in height. Anoint them with a mixture of cow dung and cow urine, and sprinkle scented water upon the steps.

Spread *nāba* grass in its proper order; place all items such as the *samidh* fuel for the *homa* on the right side, and place the *argha* vessel on the left side; prepare the various offering substances of yellow and white hues according to the requirements of the rite.
Once the fire has been lit, one should offer the impurities using the Wrathful King and invoke the Fire God.
The mantra for invoking the Fire God is as follows:

"Oṃ ehi mahābhūtani vajiṇi vijayasatvamaṅgali hite tvaṃ bhoḥ pūrvāgnaye vyākhyāyavyākhyā vahana ya svāhā. Recite this three times; this is the mantra for inviting the Fire God (*Agni*). As for the mudrā: extend the five fingers of the right hand straight upward, open the palm outward, bend the index finger toward the palm, and bend the thumb so that it rests horizontally across the palm. The movement of the thumb back and forth constitutes the mudrā for inviting the Fire God.
Please offer three sprinklings of scented water to the right and three mouthfuls of water for rinsing, while reciting this mantra three times for protection:

*Oṃ agnaye svāhā vīrya-vīrya-vahana-nibhyo nibhyaḥ svāhā*. Having completed the offering to the Fire God, sprinkle scented water again and provide water for rinsing; then, making offerings of incense, flowers, and so forth, have him sit in his original position.

Outside the steps, establish a separate place for the installation of the principal deity (iṣṭadevatā). Invite the deity according to the ritual rules and present offerings in succession. Reciting the mantra of the principal deity, place a single flower in that location and speak these words:
"I pray that the Venerable One will bestow grace upon this place and accept this homa."
Next, one should again perform the rites for the removal of impurities (*kṣāra-homa*) and so forth using the mantra and mudrā of the Wrathful King Kīlikīli.

The mantra is as follows: "Oṃ kīli kīli hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra for the removal of impurities and so forth. As for the characteristics of the mudrā: extend the five fingers of the left hand with the palm facing outward; extend the five fingers of the right hand with the palm facing inward, and join the backs of the hands together. Then, with the four fingers of the right hand—starting from the index finger—and the four fingers of the left hand, rotate the wrists downward toward the body. Finally, bring the two palms together facing each other with the two wrists joined. This is the mudrā for the removal of impurities and so forth.

The mantra for sprinkling scented water is: "Oṃ amṛte hana hana hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra for sprinkling scented water. The mantra for lighting the fire is: "Oṃ purajvala. This is the mantra for lighting the fire.

Once the impurities and the fire have been cleared away, sprinkle scented water once more, and so on, up to rinsing the mouth. Placing both hands between the two knees, first perform one *homa* offering with a ladle full of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Next, perform *homa* with the sacrificial wood; next, *homa* with the drink; next, *homa* with various grains or milk porridge; and finally, perform *homa* at will with lotuses, *karṇikāra* flowers, and so forth.
According to the specific rite, one should perform the homa with either a tranquil mind, a joyful mind, or a wrathful mind;
as for the garments worn, one should know they should be white, yellow, or red according to the rite;
and regarding the direction faced, one should act according to the rite—facing east, north, or south.
Regarding the materials for the offering, whether they be white, yellow, or red, as well as their types such as fragrance and flavor, these must also be understood.

Once the homa is completed, one should again perform a single round of homa with a ladle full of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Then, once more present the arghya water and so forth, making offerings according to the previous procedure. Again perform the protection of the body and the mudrās of the directions, as well as the protection of the deity and the protection of oneself. Finally, having performed the dissolution of the boundary (*sīmābandha*) according to the proper method, one may then dismiss [the deities].

The mudrā for dispatching the Fire Deity is the same as the mudrā for inviting the Fire Deity mentioned previously; however, one should change it so that the index finger and the thumb are pressed together—this is the mudrā for dispatching the Fire Deity.
Within the mantra for inviting the Fire God (*Agni*), by inserting the word *gaccha* (go), it becomes a mantra for dismissal; thereafter, one may act as desired.

Regarding the "five products of the cow" (*pañcagavya*)—namely, the urine of a yellow cow, its dung before it has fallen to the ground, milk, curd, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*)—as well as fragrant water from *kuśa* grass: recite each of these one hundred times, then mix them together and recite over the mixture one hundred and eight more times. On the fifteenth day of the lunar month, having fasted for one night, face eastward. Place the five products of the cow within lotus leaves or similar foliage. By silently consuming three *liang* of this, all defilements, impurities, and unclean food consumed during the fifteen days shall be purified.
First, the five purification mantras of the Buddha Family are as follows:
"Namaḥ bhagavate uṣṇīṣāya viśuddhe viraje śive śānte kṛṣe svāhā. Recite this three times; these are the five purification mantras of the Buddha Family.

The five purification mantras of the Lotus Family are as follows: "Bhagavan-māṇabhadre oṃ yaśave svāhā. Recite this three times; these are the five purification mantras of the Middle Family (Lotus Family). The five purification mantras of the Vajra Family are as follows:

"Namaḥ samantabhadra-vajrapāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpataye oṃ śikhini śikhini raṃgale pravi prabhāsa vati svasti svareti jñānavati prabhāvati svāhā. Recite this three times; this is the five-purification mantra of the Vajra Family. Furthermore, by sprinkling the five purifiers upon armlets, rosaries, waist-cords, kuśa-grass rings, sacred threads, and vajras, they all become purified.
As for the waistband, have a young girl twist and join it clockwise; after three joins, join it again three times more, making it like a web of clouds.
As for the armlets, form twenty-five vajra-knots, placing a single bead in the center with one at each end.
Regarding the encircling of the *kuśa* grass: take a length equal to the span of the ring finger and wrap it three times around [the vessel].
Form a *vajra-granthi* (vajra-knot). When eating, one may consume the food only after consecrating it by reciting the mantra of the presiding deity (*kuladevatā*) of that particular family.
When sleeping, protect the body with the *kulamātṛ* mantra; if one has a bad dream or experiences an emission of semen, one should recite the *kulamātṛ* mantra one hundred times.
One should employ the *kuleśa* mantra to protect the dwelling place, oneself, and one’s disciples, sprinkling water three times a day to purify their garments or washing them until they are clean.
At the time of eating and drinking, first recite the mantra you hold over a ball of food and offer it to the Honored One (*devatā*), and only then eat.

On all festival days, one should increase the offerings; every half-month, using an *argha* vessel, recite the *muñjakeśī* and other mantras one hundred and eight times. By thus performing self-consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one can overcome all obstacles, and accomplishment will draw near.

Three times each day, one should construct maṇḍalas and stūpas, recite Mahāyāna sūtras, contemplate the six recollections, practice meditations such as loving-kindness, circumambulate stūpas, Buddha halls, and other sacred sites, and bathe the honored images and śarīras.
